name: The A* Algorithm
statement: Find the shortest path fast by adding a heuristic guess of the remaining distance to the goal.
statementAccent: adding a heuristic guess of the remaining distance to the goal
meaning: A*, pronounced A-star, is a graph traversal and pathfinding algorithm that finds the shortest path between a start node and a goal node. It is an informed search, or best-first search, algorithm, meaning it uses a heuristic to guide its exploration toward the goal, which makes it more efficient than uninformed algorithms like Dijkstra's on many problems. A* chooses which node to expand next by minimizing the function f of n equals g of n plus h of n, where g of n is the actual cost of the path from the start node to node n, and h of n is a heuristic estimate of the cost from n to the goal. In this way it combines the strengths of Dijkstra's algorithm, which uses only g of n and so guarantees correctness, with those of greedy best-first search, which uses only h of n and so heads toward the goal. A* is guaranteed to find the least-cost path provided the heuristic h is admissible, meaning it never overestimates the true remaining cost; if h is also consistent, or monotone, A* is optimally efficient among comparable algorithms. If the heuristic is zero everywhere, A* reduces to Dijkstra's algorithm. It was developed in 1968 by Peter Hart, Nils Nilsson, and Bertram Raphael at the Stanford Research Institute, in the paper A Formal Basis for the Heuristic Determination of Minimum Cost Paths, as part of the Shakey the robot project. A* is one of the most widely used search algorithms, in video-game pathfinding, robotics, and navigation.
mechanism: A* finds a shortest path by expanding nodes in order of a combined cost that balances how far it has already travelled against how far it estimates it still has to go. For each node n it maintains two quantities: g of n, the actual cost of the best path found so far from the start to n, and h of n, a heuristic estimate of the cost from n to the goal. It expands nodes in increasing order of their sum, f of n equals g of n plus h of n, always choosing the frontier node with the smallest f. This is the key to its efficiency: the g term keeps the search honest, ensuring it accounts for real distance travelled as Dijkstra's algorithm does, while the h term steers exploration toward the goal as greedy best-first search does, so A* avoids expanding large regions of the graph that lead away from the target. The behaviour and guarantees depend on the heuristic. If h never overestimates the true remaining cost, it is called admissible, and A* is then guaranteed to return an optimal, least-cost path. If h additionally satisfies a consistency, or monotonicity, condition, A* never needs to reopen a settled node and is optimally efficient among admissible algorithms of its kind. The extreme case h equals zero removes all guidance and reduces A* exactly to Dijkstra's algorithm, which explores uniformly outward. On grids, common admissible heuristics are the straight-line Euclidean distance and, for four-directional movement, the Manhattan distance. Choosing a heuristic that is admissible yet as close as possible to the true cost is what makes A* both correct and fast.

examples.text: A* expands the node with the smallest f of n equals g of n plus h of n, cost so far plus estimated cost to go.
If h never overestimates the remaining cost, A* is guaranteed to find the least-cost path.
With a zero heuristic, A* becomes Dijkstra's algorithm, exploring uniformly outward.

whyItMatters: A* is one of the most important and widely used algorithms in computer science and artificial intelligence, the standard method for finding shortest paths when a good estimate of remaining distance is available. Its applications are everywhere: it moves characters and units around in video games, plans routes for robots and autonomous vehicles, computes directions in navigation and mapping systems, and solves search and planning problems throughout artificial intelligence. Its enduring importance comes from a simple, powerful idea, adding a heuristic estimate of the distance still to go to the cost already incurred, which lets it focus its search toward the goal and so run far faster than uninformed methods while still guaranteeing an optimal path when the heuristic is admissible. This blend of efficiency and optimality, together with clean and well-understood theoretical guarantees, has made A* a foundational tool and a staple of algorithms and AI education, and it generalizes Dijkstra's algorithm, which is simply A* with no heuristic. Developed in 1968 by Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael for the pioneering Shakey robot, it has remained the go-to pathfinding algorithm for more than half a century. As the method that finds shortest paths quickly by adding a heuristic guess of the remaining distance, A* is a cornerstone of computing.

working.text: compute f of n equals g of n, cost from the start, plus h of n, the heuristic estimate to the goal.
always expand the frontier node with the smallest f, balancing progress against direction.
with an admissible heuristic, the first path found to the goal is guaranteed least-cost.

limits: A* is powerful but its guarantees depend on conditions that reward care. Its optimality holds only when the heuristic h is admissible, never overestimating the true remaining cost; an inadmissible heuristic can make A* faster but may return a non-optimal path. The consistency, or monotonicity, condition is stronger and ensures no node needs reopening; admissible-but-inconsistent heuristics are handled with more care. A* can also be memory-intensive, since it must keep all generated nodes on its frontier and in its explored set, which for large graphs can be prohibitive, motivating memory-bounded variants. The quality of the heuristic determines everything: a weak heuristic close to zero makes A* behave like Dijkstra's algorithm and explore widely, while a strong one focuses the search, so designing good admissible heuristics is the real art. Some details reward care: A* was published in 1968 by Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael, the paper's exact title is A Formal Basis for the Heuristic Determination of Minimum Cost Paths, and Manhattan distance is the same as taxicab distance. So A* robustly finds shortest paths with a heuristic, understood as an algorithm whose optimality requires admissibility and whose speed and memory depend on the heuristic's quality.
misreadings: A* is not guaranteed optimal with any heuristic; the heuristic must be admissible, never overestimating the remaining cost. It is not free of cost, since it can consume large memory holding its frontier. And a poor heuristic makes it no better than Dijkstra's algorithm, so treating A* as optimal regardless of heuristic, as memory-cheap, or as always faster than uninformed search, misreads it.
origin: The informed pathfinding algorithm published by Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael in 1968 for the Shakey robot, which finds shortest paths by minimizing path cost so far plus a heuristic estimate of the cost to the goal.
